structure.title: The proposed act
structure.text: The opening follows Raskolnikov's reasoning amid poverty, overheard stories, and family pressure.

structure.title: Living afterwards
structure.text: Six parts and an epilogue explore the collision between private explanation, other people's needs, and official investigation.

people.name: Raskolnikov
people.text: A proud, penniless former law student in St Petersburg, who has talked himself into a theory that a superior man may step over the law.

people.name: Razumikhin
people.text: A cheerful, energetic fellow student who keeps turning up to help Raskolnikov, whether or not he wants it.

people.name: Sonya
people.text: The gentle daughter of a drunken clerk, forced into prostitution to feed her family, whose faith survives everything.

context.title: Names and intimacy
context.text: Rodion Romanovich, Raskolnikov, and Rodya refer to the same man. Formal and affectionate names signal different relationships.
context.takeaway: Track people through relationships, not spelling alone.

context.title: Exceptional individuals
context.text: Raskolnikov considers whether extraordinary achievement can justify stepping over moral prohibitions. The novel tests his distinction through lived encounters.
context.takeaway: His theory is a claim under examination.

notice.why: Fever, exhaustion, and involuntary gestures complicate deliberate self-control.
People's actions resist the categories used to explain them.

opening: Raskolnikov has an argument for murder. The woman he intends to kill is a predatory pawnbroker; her money could finance a useful life, and great men have done worse for less. He wants to know whether he belongs among those who can step over the law. Dostoevsky follows him from the argument into the deed and its aftermath, where an ordinary conversation can become unbearable and the need to conceal what he has done begins competing with the need for someone to know.
